source.title: Redundant representations help generalization in wide neural networks ,
source.authors: Diego Doimo; Aldo Glielmo; Sebastian Goldt; A. Laio

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent truncation.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests how width, weight decay, and training to interpolation relate to test error and representation redundancy, using chunking and reconstruction analyses rather than the original claim’s random-label memorization comparison.
record.gate_note: The study measures natural-label test error across model widths and random neuron chunks, and tests how weight decay and interpolation affect that behavior. Results cited from earlier work, including random-label fitting, are not rows. Other reported properties such as reconstruction R² and residual correlation are included only where they bear on tested versions.
record.test_reason: The study directly measures training and test error across network widths, finding continued test-error reductions beyond interpolation in deeper, explicitly regularized networks. This tests V2 in new settings. Chunk ablations and reconstruction analyses investigate a proposed mechanism rather than independently testing V2.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. The authors propose redundant, approximately independent representations as a possible mechanism for improved generalization in wide, regularized networks. Clone signatures appear in their interpolating examples and fail without weight decay or in their non-interpolating ImageNet models. The experiments do not establish that this mechanism is necessary for every width-related generalization improvement.
record.recipe_differences: Uses weight decay, SGD with momentum for convolutional models and Adam for fully connected MNIST models; studies natural-label generalization and random chunks of trained representations rather than random-label fitting. Also uses augmentation and label smoothing in CIFAR and ImageNet setups.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome depends on weight decay, reaching zero training error, training duration, dataset, architecture, and whether intermediate or only final-layer width is increased.

fits_no_version.finding: Large random chunks reproduce full-network performance and permit accurate reconstruction with weakly correlated residuals; these signatures depend on regularization and interpolation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wide, regularized interpolating networks can develop redundant final representations that provide a possible mechanism for improved generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Further training after the full network interpolates improves chunk training accuracy and slightly lowers full-network test error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generalization can continue improving during training after zero full-network training error is reached.

fits_no_version.finding: Widening only the final layer of a network described as unable to interpolate leaves test error approximately constant.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Final-layer widening alone can fail to improve generalization when intermediate representations remain insufficient.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2022 (36th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems; supplied metadata lists 2021)
record.problems: The paper reports error bars in its checklist, but the supplied main text does not specify them for the extracted results. Several result curves are described qualitatively without numeric values. ImageNet models do not interpolate, limiting comparison with the CIFAR and pMNIST clone regime. The supplied text contains a discrepancy between the stated W=704 for DenseNet40-BC and the methods formula W=5.5·c, which gives W=1408 at c=256.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result rows beyond the 9 extracted; cited prior-work results were omitted. Figure-only exact values were not read from plots.

untested.parts: No own random-label fitting experiment or natural-label versus random-label held-out comparison.
The original one-hidden-layer ReLU setting, absence of explicit regularization, and training to convergence are not reproduced. The results do not establish the test-error peak near interpolation.
No controlled convolutional versus fully connected comparison on the same image task, or intervention on local connectivity.
No optimizer comparison on a shared workload under controlled tuning.
No batch-size intervention comparing held-out performance.
No dropout training intervention; post-training neuron removal does not test dropout's generalization benefit.
No magnitude-aware weight sharpness measurements or ranking of generalization gaps.
No removal of memorized training examples or matched random-example removal.

missing.what: Separate CIFAR100 full-network width sweep: accuracy is 70.4%, 75.7%, 79.6%, 80.8%, and 81.9% for WR28-1, -2, -4, -8, and -16. Pair these results with the full-network training-error curve rather than chunk results.

FC5 pMNIST full-network width sweep showing decreasing test error in the wide interpolating regime. The task is parity classification after projection onto ten principal components, with weight decay and an appendix that names Adam.
missing.locator: Sections 2.1 and 3; Figures 2 and 4-a; Appendix A

missing.what: Additional width sweeps trained on 10,000-example subsets with fixed regularization show decreasing test loss at larger widths and declining variance after peaks at W=32, 64, and 88. These are distinct from the main full-data accuracy sweeps and support the wider-network trend, although the supplied figure text does not independently locate their interpolation thresholds.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V2. Explicit regularization and different architectures define the tested extension; they are not themselves negative results. Neither failure of a particular chunk scaling exponent nor failure to interpolate warrants a limits_scope verdict on V2.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of natural-label and random-label test accuracy.
Does not test one-hidden-layer ReLU networks on MNIST and downsampled CIFAR-10 as specified; tests several architectures and datasets, with width and regularization conditions.
No controlled convolutional versus fully connected comparison of image generalization.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD generalization comparison.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare sharpness to norm- or margin-based measures.
Does not remove memorized examples or compare with random-example removal.

rows.subject: Wide-ResNet-28 for CIFAR10
rows.operation_detail: Test error of full networks across width approaches ensemble error approximately as W^-1/2.

conditions.value: SGD with momentum and weight decay

rows.baseline: error∞, error of an ensemble average of 20 networks of the widest size
rows.note: Authors report the width-related decline for full networks; this is not a one-hidden-layer ReLU sweep.
rows.check: This is a family-level width sweep, not a result for W=512 alone. Table 1 reports CIFAR10 accuracy increasing from 84.1% to 96.1% across WR28 widths. Weight decay is used, and label smoothing varies with width.

source_check.correct: The scaling describes the CIFAR10 Wide-ResNet28 width sweep, not W=512 alone. W=512 identifies WR28-8, also used for chunk experiments. Training lasts 200 epochs; label smoothing varies across widths.
source_check.locator_found: Figure 2; section 2.1; Figure 3 caption; Appendix A.
source_check.problem: A family-level scaling relation is attached to a single checkpoint.

rows.subject: Wide-ResNet-28 for CIFAR10
rows.stage_stated: trained, no fine-tuning after chunk selection
rows.operation_detail: Randomly select wc last-layer neurons and set all other last-layer activations to zero.

conditions.value: wc > wc*; threshold depends on dataset and architecture
500 random neuron subsets per chunk width

rows.measure: Chunk test error relative to error∞
rows.baseline: error∞, error of an ensemble of 20 widest networks
rows.value: For wc > wc*, test error decays as wc^-1/2, following the same law as full networks of the same width.
rows.note: The text states the relationship and that chunk error matches an independently trained full network of width wc in this regime.
rows.check: Increasing a retained chunk of an already trained network is not widening independently trained networks beyond their interpolation threshold. The reported chunk scaling is valid but does not directly measure V2.

rows.subject: Wide-ResNet-28 for CIFAR100
rows.stage_stated: trained, no fine-tuning after chunk selection
rows.operation_detail: Randomly select wc last-layer neurons and set the rest of their activations to zero.

conditions.value: 500 random neuron subsets per chunk width

rows.measure: Chunk test error relative to ensemble error
rows.baseline: error∞, error of an ensemble of 20 widest networks
rows.value: For sufficiently large chunks, test error decays approximately with the same law as independent networks of the same width; error − error∞ ∝ W^-1/2 across widths and architectures.
rows.note: Appendix describes clone size as 128/256 and says test accuracy for W > 128/256 decays approximately with the independent-network law.
rows.check: The row conflates chunk ablation with full-network width scaling. Separate the full-network CIFAR100 results into a V2 row. Figure 3 uses the widest W=1024 network; Appendix Figure S1 instead describes WR28-8, with W=512.

rows.subject: DenseNet40-BC (k=128)
rows.operation_detail: Test error of full networks across width approaches ensemble error approximately as W^-1/2.

conditions.value: SGD with momentum and weight decay

rows.baseline: error∞, error of an ensemble average of 20 widest networks (Fig. 2)
rows.note: Width W is 5.5·c; for k=128, c=256 and W=1408 in the described setup. The paper’s text gives the family-level relation rather than a separate numerical value for this checkpoint.
rows.check: Represent this as a DenseNet40-BC family sweep. At k=128, c=256 and W=1408, not 704. The introduction explicitly reports zero training error above approximately W=350 and continued test-error decline. Table 1 gives accuracy increasing from 91.6% to 96.0% across the family.

source_check.correct: The scaling describes the DenseNet40-BC family sweep. W=5.5c and c=2k, so k=128 gives W=1408; W=704 corresponds to k=64. Networks wider than approximately 350 reach zero training error while test error continues decreasing.
source_check.problem: The checkpoint width is incorrect, and the scaling belongs to the family sweep.

rows.subject: Wide-ResNet-28-8
rows.operation_detail: Compare chunk test error with and without weight decay.

conditions.value: same architecture and dataset with weight decay

rows.baseline: With weight decay, chunk error scales as wc^-1/2.
rows.value: Without weight decay, chunk error does not scale as wc^-1/2.
rows.note: The authors state the scaling signature does not appear without regularization.
rows.check: Failure of the inverse-square-root chunk scaling law does not establish failure of test-error improvement with full-network width. This is evidence about clone formation without weight decay, not an absent V2 effect.

rows.subject: Wide-ResNet-28-8
rows.stage_stated: epoch 160: full network reaches zero training error; later training continues
rows.operation_detail: Track full and chunk test error during training after the full model reaches zero training error.
rows.baseline: Test error at epoch 160; numeric value not stated
rows.value: Both training phases lead to a reduction in test error; after epoch 180 test error stops improving.
rows.note: This tracks training over epochs rather than a width sweep; test error improves as clones form and then plateaus.
rows.check: The intervention is additional training at fixed width. A small test-error improvement after interpolation does not measure the effect of widening.

rows.subject: ResNet50-4
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate random chunks from the last hidden representation of the widest network.
rows.measure: Chunk test-error scaling and training error
rows.baseline: error∞, error of an ensemble of four ResNet50-4 networks
rows.value: Largest model training top-1 error is approximately 8%; chunk test-error scaling is steeper than wc^-1/2.
rows.note: This is an extension to a setting where the model does not interpolate; the authors say redundant clones are not observed.
rows.check: The largest ImageNet model still has approximately 8% training error, so the sweep never establishes V2's post-interpolation condition. Steeper chunk-error scaling is not partial evidence for V2.

rows.subject: ResNet28-1 with modified final block
rows.operation_detail: Increase only the final-layer channel count while holding the rest of the network width constant.
rows.baseline: Test error of modified ResNet28-1 at lower final-layer width
rows.value: Test error is approximately constant as only the final-layer width increases.
rows.note: The result shows that increasing only final-layer width is insufficient when the overall network remains narrow.
rows.check: The discussion explicitly describes this network as too narrow to interpolate. Constant test error under final-layer-only widening therefore does not challenge continued improvement beyond interpolation.

rows.subject: DenseNet40-BC with 1 × 1 convolution bottleneck
rows.operation_detail: Increase intermediate-layer width while holding final representation width fixed.
rows.value: Test accuracy of the full network decays approximately as wc^-1/2; 16 random neurons suffice to interpolate training error < 5 · 10^-3.
rows.note: The appendix says increasing intermediate widths yields the scaling even with final-layer width fixed.
rows.check: Separate full-network intermediate-width scaling from chunk interpolation and reconstruction. The appendix's statement that test accuracy decays is inconsistent with its test-error framing and the discussion; report decreasing test error qualitatively. With final width fixed, the full-network width sweep should not be expressed using chunk width wc. The reported chunk training error below 0.005 is near-zero, not exactly zero.
